title: Three palaces
hookLine: one for the rains, one for winter, one for summer; "I was delicately nurtured" (AN 3.38)
last: THE SWAN — LIFE BELONGS TO WHO PROTECTS IT.

lines: SO MUCH COMFORT, NO REASON TO LEAVE.
cards: Remember Kondañña's one raised finger, and the king who hoped his son would stay home and rule? This is where the king acts on that hope.

If the boy is going to leave because he sees the world's pain, the reasoning goes, then make sure he never sees it. Wrap him in so much comfort that he never has a reason to look past the garden wall.
And for years, it works. Today, in the Buddha's own words, what it was like to grow up that way.

teach.h: BLUE, RED AND WHITE LOTUS PONDS.
teach.b: In one of the discourses, the Buddha looks back on his youth. He says he was raised delicately. His father had lotus ponds made just for him, one of blue lotuses, one of red, one of white.

His clothes were made of cloth from Kasi, the country around Benares. A white parasol was held over him day and night, so that cold and heat, dust and grass and dew wouldn't touch him. And he had three palaces.
One for the cold season, one for the hot season, one for the rainy season.
During the four months of rain, he says, he stayed up in the rainy-season palace, surrounded by musicians, and never once came down.
Even the servants in his father's house ate fine rice and meat, where in other houses servants got broken rice and sour gruel. No humble origin story: he grew up rich, and he says so.
But then, in the same passage, the tone changes. He says: amid all that, a thought came to him. Ordinary, untaught people see someone old, and they're disgusted, forgetting that they'll grow old too.
The same with sickness. The same with death.

teach.h: THE PRIDE OF YOUTH FELL AWAY.
teach.b: And when he saw that, he says, the pride of youth, the pride of health, the pride of being alive, all fell away from him. The three palaces kept out the rain, the heat, the cold. They couldn't keep out that thought.
Comfort isn't a bad thing. But it can be a wall. And walls, sooner or later, have gates.

how: Buddhists retell the Buddha's sheltered youth as the setting for his going forth; the Sukhamala Sutta, where he describes it, is studied as a teaching on the three intoxications of youth, health and life.

o: The Buddha's seasonal homes from a sheltered youth
Three temples a king built after the awakening
The halls where the Buddha first taught his monks

games.q: what's inside the palace — tap the pairs.
p: held over him day and night
fell away when he saw aging

s: the Buddha hid his wealthy upbringing
he describes it himself, in detail: the lotus ponds, the parasol, the three palaces.
the servants in his father's house ate fine rice and meat
where servants elsewhere got broken rice and sour gruel, he says.
the palaces kept every hard thought away
a thought about aging, sickness and death got through, and his pride of youth fell away.

games.q: you're a king who's been told your son will leave home if he sees the world's pain. what do you do, in the story?
o: tell him everything, and let him choose.
surround him with so much comfort he never looks past the wall.
send him to study far away.
games.why: the king builds a wall of comfort: three palaces, lotus ponds, music. and for years it works, until a thought gets through.

practice: Let the breath settle, then look around for one comfort you forgot you had: a roof in the rain, warm water from a tap, a chair that holds you, glasses that let you see.

Notice it the way the Buddha noticed his palaces, and feel a little gratitude for it. Then gently ask: is there anything it's keeping me from seeing? You don't need an answer; let the question sit beside the gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Three palaces. One for the cold, one for the heat, one for the rains: the comfort the Buddha grew up in, and the thought that got through anyway.

orig.note: Pali: a palace or mansion, the word used for the three seasonal palaces.

carryVoice: Your line: comfort can be a wall. A gentle line to keep beside your gratitude. See you tomorrow.
